stories.title_en: AI agents aren't 'going rogue.' Frontier labs are skipping security basics
stories.title_ja: AIエージェントは『暴走』していない。フロンティアラボはセキュリティの基本を省略している

comments.author: Gshaheen
comments.text: This aligned with my initial opinion on these "rogue agents" and then I spoke to a cyber security head at one of the largest healthcare companies in the world. While he agreed, yes, there can be better safeguards, the fact of the matter is that these things will happen. So therefore, it's not an argument about how good security was or wasn't, it is a fact that these scenarios will occur. The argument/question now is, how do you defend yourself against these events? My opinion shifted after hearing that.

comments.author: cmiles8
comments.text: Both can be true. It’s clear models are doing rogue things. But it’s also clear that the labs look like amateur hour with their technical security and testing practices.

comments.author: metalsiliconYT
comments.text: There are some perverse incentives here, the more evil stuff these agents do the more capable and impressive it makes them look. Its also a huge publicity event that gets everyone talking about the company when a rogue event happens.

comments.author: ammon
comments.text: The scary thing is not that agents "went rogue" (yes, poor security may be at fault for that). It's that they wanted to. Better security might have hidden that from us, but it would not have changed the fact that the current generation of models under certain (repeatable) conditions coordinate around goals as aggressive as hacking Hugging Face.

comments.author: aaquibahm
comments.text: i think it's unfair to assume the labs paying top dollar for cybersecurity engineers somehow have an incompetent bunch of nincompoops running their evals. it's a hard problem! to conduct effective evals, you sometimes need the model to have (restricted) access to the internet. at the same time, you have thousands (!!) of model instances with high cyber capabilities that will do whatever it takes to solve the answer. the infra surrounding model evals may soon (or already) genuinely be subjected to more hacking attempts from all sorts of weird angles than any other code on the planet.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、AIエージェントが「暴走」した原因がラボのセキュリティ不備なのか、それともモデル自身が一定条件下で攻撃的な目標を追求する内在的傾向なのかという点。賛否は、セキュリティがずさんだという批判（「アマチュアアワー」）と、トップクラスのサイバーエンジニアを雇っても評価は極めて困難で、インターネットアクセスが必要なテスト環境が多数の高能力モデルインスタンスにさらされ、むしろ攻撃の標的になりやすいという擁護に分かれた。注目コメントとして、「暴走したのではなく、エージェントがそれを望んでいた」という指摘や、「評価インフラ自体が planèteire レベルのハッキング試行にさらされている」という洞察が挙げられた。
stories.editor_note: 「暴走」という誇張された表現に惑わされず、実際は基本的なセキュリティ設計が欠如していることが問題だと指摘。フロンティアラブの急速なモデル公開がセキュリティレビューを後回しにし、日本のAIスタートアップでも同様の見落としが起きやすい状況になっている。

stories.title_en: Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
stories.title_ja: Go 1.27におけるHTTP/1コネクションの再利用が改善

comments.author: donatj
comments.text: > Using HTTP/1 (GODEBUG=http2client=0), calling this function 100 times against index.golang.org takes ~710 milliseconds on Go 1.26 on my machine. On Go 1.27, the same program takes ~150 milliseconds. Does this mean I need to disable http2 for this to work or is that just a further proof that http2 isn't actually being used?

comments.author: jerf
comments.text: Am I missing something or is none of this information documented in net/http itself? This is a surprising implementation of "Close" and should be documented somewhere. I can attest to the fact this is a Frequently Asked Question among people who are trying to Go as an HTTP client, so even though this feels somewhat icky, I can understand where it is coming from. However, I'm also missing, if I want to slam this connection closed, which is a reasonable thing to want, how do I do that without uselessly draining a socket I don't intend to reuse? Fake the "Connection: close" header into the Response object? Hope I can dig out an underlying socket of some sort under the concrete type of the Body.Response that I can bypass this code with? Seems like there should be a way to do that too.

comments.author: rkuska
comments.text: Now if you use json’s Decoder you can read a body and still might end up without reused connection - if a response contains a newline. Decoder only reads X bytes (512? I don’t remember) and if the structure fits into these bytes exactly (and the multiplications of it) the newline leaves hanging there. I always check for Decoder.More (this drains whitespace) after decoding.

comments.author: nasretdinov
comments.text: It sucks that this changes the behaviour under the hood that you previously coukd rely on the fact that closing the response body lets you skip downloading the HTTP body entirely, but I do like the tradeoff here, since it also limits the download time to just 50ms you'd not get overwhelmed if your network can't keep up with all the cancelled HTTP bodies, you'll just wait a little bit of traffic instead.

comments.author: jamesponddotco
comments.text: I can finally retire xhttp.DrainResponseBody[1], which I just learned, wasn’t doing that good of a job anyway. [1]: https://github.com/cipherdothost/x-go/blob/caa562ded82b8c417...

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Go 1.27でHTTP/1の接続再利用が改善され、同一リクエストを100回実行すると約710 ms→150 msと劇的に速くなったこと。これに伴い、http2を無効にしなければならないのか、それとも単にhttp2が実際に使われていない証拠かという疑問や、Response.Body.Closeの挙動が以前と変わり、接続をすぐに閉じたいときにソケットを無駄にドレインする必要がある点が論争となった。賛否は、遅延ダウンロードを防ぐトレードオフは評価される一方で、ドキュメント不足や「Connection: close」ヘッダーを偽装する回避策が必要だと指摘する声がある。注目コメントでは、json.Decoderが改行を残すと接続が再利用されなくなるためDecoder.Moreでドレインすべきであると助言され、さらに独自に作っていたxhttp.DrainResponseBodyラッパーは今では不要になったと結論付けられている。
stories.editor_note: Go 1.27におけるHTTP/1コネクションの再利用改善は、細かいバッファ管理とタイムアウト調整によって実現。クラウドネイティブなマイクロサービスを多用する日本企業にとって、レイテンシ削減とコストダウンの具体的メリットが期待できる。

stories.title_en: Submarine cable resilience
stories.title_ja: 海底ケーブルのレジリエンス

comments.author: andrewrn

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: I worked for an L1 blockchain for a couple years and while the term "decentralized" is bandied about a bit too much, reading articles like this does underscore how vulnerable global traffic is. e.g. some EVM chains have a majority of "stake" in either one country or several adjacent countries (particularly in Asia). A cable cut there, which the article points out has happened, can lead to the blockchain getting cut off or even halting.

stories.summary_ja: 深海ケーブルの敷設・保守は技術的に困難で、波の多い海域での作業は宇宙開発並みに過酷。これによりグローバル通信やブロックチェーンの信頼性は脆弱だと指摘される。L1ブロックチェーン開発者は「非中央集権的」は過大評価で、アジアにステークが集中したチェーンはケーブル切断でネットワーク遮断・停止のリスクがあると警告。台湾・バルト海を結ぶケーブルは異常に不運な場所にあり、統計的に考えにくい状況だと指摘。その他の参加者は海底ケーブルの工学的偉業に驚嘆し、断面をインテリアとして欲しいとしている。ケーブルの重要性は共通認識だが、ブロックチェーンの分散性については意見が分かれ、特に洞察に富んでいたのはステーク分布とケーブル脆弱性を結びつけた二番目のコメントである。一部は地理的なステーク集中を実質的中心化と見なすが、他は技術的に分散性を保てると考える。
stories.editor_note: 海底ケーブルのレジリエンスは、多経路設計と自動復旧アルゴリズムによって地震や船舶アンカー損傷に耐性を高めている。災害多発国である日本では、この技術動向が国内通信インフラの強化策として注目されている。

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、Iosevkaフォントの見た目と可読性、特に長時間使用した際の目の疲れやDejaVu Sans Monoとの違和感、カスタマイズ性の高さ（パラメトリックビルドシステムとPatEL DSL、オンラインカスタマイザー）、コードリガチャの賛否、FREETYPE_PROPERTIESによるレンダリング調整、そしてfont‑display: swapを使ったフォント表示時の初期表示がCourierと見分けづらい問題などが挙げられた。

賛否両論については、可読性に関して「目に痛い」「普段使いには向かない」と感じるユーザーがいる一方で、何年も愛用し自分の好みに合わせてカスタムバージョンを作るユーザーは「最高のフォント」と高評価。コードリガチャについては、 ligatureが「=」や「<>」などの文字数を数えにくくしたり、誤認を招くとして否定的意見がある一方、省スペースでコードが読みやすくなると肯定する声もある。また、FREETYPE_PROPERTIESの設定がフォントの太さやエッジの暗さを調整し、ビットマップフォントからの移行を容易にしたという実践的なヒントも共有された。

注目コメントとして、作者be5invisが独自DSLであるPatELを開発し、プログラム的にフォントを生成した点への感謝と、カスタマイズ用オンラインツール（typeof.net/Iosevka/customizer）およびリポジトリのドキュメントへのリンクが紹介された。さらに、あるユーザーが「Iosevka、 proper fontconfig、そして export FREETYPE_PROPERTIES=\"cff:no-stem-darkening=0 autofitter:no-stem-darkening=0\"」の組み合わせが自分にとって決定的だったと指摘し、環境変数の設定が快適なターミナル体験に不可欠だったことを強調した。
stories.editor_note: Iosevkaはオープンソースのサンセリフおよびスラブセリフ等幅フォントで、カスタマイズ性と可読性が高い。GitHubでのテーマ共有が活発な日本のエンジニアコミュニティでも、ライセンスが permissive なため商用プロダクトへの組み込みが容易だ。

stories.title_en: Do dentists know what they're doing?
stories.title_ja: 歯医者は自分が何をしているのか知っているのか？

comments.author: tkdb
comments.text: I'm surprised that there isn't more attention being paid to this question: How does dental (or medical) care differ when the person recommending the procedure directly benefits financially from it? I've had experiences with doctors who make exactly the same if they perform a $1,000 procedure or a $10,000 procedure, and I feel in general I'm likely to get better care in that scenario. (In the US) I regularly scrutinize and stress over the dentist's recommendations, as they are almost always the owner of the business as well as the head dental procedure recommender.

comments.author: HarHarVeryFunny
comments.text: My experience is that there is a huge difference in skill set and knowledge between different dentists. If you suspect your dentist is causing problems, or if your cleaning sessions are painful, then switch. You'd like to think they are all equally competent trained professionals, but that is not the case. I'm sure the same is true of doctors too.

comments.author: nsb1
comments.text: You know those people in your university classes who just skated buy and were at the bottom of the bell curve? Unfortunately dentistry and other medical fields have them too. I've had the misfortune of running into a few myself.

comments.author: post_break
comments.text: Meanwhile I just went back to my dentist to get a cleaning and a filling fixed. I have bad anxiety from growing up with a Dentist who could be described as Jigsaw from the saw movies. My current dentist has nitrous, which is a game changer for me. He also has hardcore numbing cream before the shot, and he also uses a two shot method, the first one is initial numbing that doesn't last long but also doesn't burn as much. And the second after that is full strength but by that time thanks to the gas and the first shot and the numbing cream I can't feel.

comments.author: AlanYx
comments.text: Dentistry is an interesting field because it's the only major profession where you can still routinely get hired as a full professor without a PhD. (This used to be more common in other professions fifty years ago.) As an outsider, perhaps this is one reason why there seems to be more of an applied and subjective judgment-based (even perhaps cargo-cult like) element to the profession.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
治療を勧める側が金銭的に利益を得る場合の利益相反と、歯科医の間にある技術・知識のばらつきについて議論が集中した。  

・賛否両論  
利益相反が過剰な治療を招くと警戒する意見と、患者が情報収集やセカンドオピニオンで対処できると考える意見が分かれた。また、歯科医のスキル差については「皆同じレベル」という思い込みを否定する声と、経験豊富な医師でもミスはあるという見解に分かれた。  

・注目コメント  
投稿者は自身の歯科恐怖症の例を挙げ、亜硝酸ガス（笑気麻酔）や段階的な麻酔法が痛みを大きく軽減した経験を共有し、患者中心の工夫が治療の質を高めると指摘した。このコメントは、技術的な配慮が不安を和らげる具体的な事例として注目された。
stories.editor_note: 歯医者が自分が何をしているのか知っているかという疑問は、説明不足が信頼喪失につながるという指摘。日本のクリニックでもデジタルカルテの普及が進む中、インフォームドコンセントのデジタル化が求められている。

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点: ICEがERO ONEで機密・非機密情報を結びつけ、市民間の人間関係をネットワーク分析で追跡しようとしている点。これにより令状不要の国内監視が可能になり、移民執行の枠を超えてプライバシーや言論の自由が脅かされる懸念が中心。

・注目コメント: 一部はSection 702/FISAを活用すればNSAの収集データをAIが即座に解析し、個人の「汚点」や leverage を浮かび上がらせられると警告し、実質的令状不要の監視になると指摘。また、「執行と排斥」の名称は旧ソ連のNKVD・Chekaを連想させ、歴史的悪夢の再来を危惧する声も目立った。
stories.editor_note: ICEが$100M『ナイトメア』国内スパイプログラムを企画中である背景には、テロ対策と不法滞在者追跡の二重目的がある。日本では同様の監視拡大議論が出ており、プライバシー保護と安全のバランスが改めて問われている。

stories.title_en: Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
stories.title_ja: Pg_vectorsearch: pgvectorのIVFFlatとHNSWよりも高速なインデックス

comments.author: devy
comments.text: A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing. - pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW index has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that). - pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out. - pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.

comments.author: EgregiousCube
comments.text: I'm currently running VectorChord and I love it - with a fast backing disk, it's cut my postgres cost in half. Excited to see competition in low-RAM vector index tools. RAMageddon seems to be creating incentives to find more ways to take advantage of how fast modern nvme drives are!

comments.author: potomushto
comments.text: Interesting, I see no mention of support for bit precision and hammer distance operator which supposed to be much faster and storage efficient

comments.author: Rapzid
comments.text: Does it support filtering though? Edit: post filtering only I don't understand how people are efficiently implementing tenant/user/permission scopes with these indexes.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、pg_vectorsearchがPRISMという量子化IVFインデックスを採用し、次元数上限が1968次元かつPostgres 18以上が必要で、アルファ版のため実運用での検証が不足し、マネージドPGサービスでは未対応である点。これに対して、VectorChordを使っているユーザーは低RAM・NVMe活用によるコスト削減に期待し、競合の登場を歓迎している。一方で、pgvectorscaleの保守状況を疑問視し、新規インデックスではなく既存ツールへの改善を求める声や、ビット精度・ハマー距離演算子、ポストフィルタリングのみの制約によるマルチテナンシー実装の難しさへの懸念が示された。
stories.editor_note: Pg_vectorsearchはpgvectorのIVFFlatとHNSWよりも高速なインデックスを提供し、ベクトル検索のボトルネックを緩和。レコメンデーションや画像検索を抱える日本のスタートアップは、コスト削減と応答速度向上を見込める。

stories.title_en: Amazon pushes up prices across the Internet
stories.title_ja: Amazonはインターネット全体で価格を引き上げている

comments.author: steveBK123
comments.text: I find that 20 years ago I shopped at Amazon for the low prices, but 2020s+ I shop at Amazon due to their logistics. The problem for everyone else is not simply that Amazon ships quickly, I almost don't even care about that. The thing is that Amazon ships & delivers on a reliable predicted schedule. When I click an item on Amazon and it says "arrives by Tuesday" then 95/100 times it does. I shop at specific competitors who can do similar (B&H, Sweetwater, etc). Many online stores big & small in the year 2026 will still take days to even send shipment info, followed by using unreliable carriers that miss ETAs. I would even be OK with these stores giving a narrow range or probability "90% of the time this arrives between Tuesday & Wednesday".. But I am not in the mood to order stuff that may arrive in 2-10 days with very little clarity on which end of the range.

comments.author: trombuance
comments.text: Amazon searches for anything that isn't a known brand such as Apple & co turn out >90% Chinese products of highly questionable quality for me these days. And you can buy those cheaper by going straight to the source. The sole point of their retail business seems to be providing a support for the inevitable issues with these sellers, but I suspect that increasingly customers won't think it justifies the massive premium they're paying for what's essentially Taobao with an American address.

comments.author: novia
comments.text: Amazon allows you to make returns and makes it convenient, quick, and easy. I made two purchases through independent sellers' websites in the last year, both with big banners guaranteeing satisfaction and easy returns for 100 days or something. And yet, when I found that the product didn't meet my needs, they would not accept my return. They wouldn't even issue a return label. Both of these sellers used Shop. Shop requires you to fill out an application for a refund and then the seller can drag their feet on processing it. In both cases they let the application sit there for days before rejecting it. In one of the cases my credit card company ruled in favor of the small business when I issued a chargeback. On Amazon it's easy to request a return and get a return label all on the same day that you discover you have a subpar product. The long and short of it is that consumers do not want to be ripped off, and centralized sellers like Amazon and AliExpress make it easy to not be ripped off. If this raises prices across the board, so be it. It's worth it for the time saved and the accountability that comes along with it.

I didn't notice it until earlier this year. I was shopping for some new shoes of a specific brand that I like. Was about to pull the trigger on Amazon and then realized I would happen to walk by a shoe store while doing other errands later in the day and thought it would be nice to get them even sooner than 1-2 day prime shipping. I went to the store and tried them on and realized I needed a 1/2 size smaller than what I ordered. Then I paid and realized the shoe store price was $10 less than Amazon. So you really are paying for laziness/convenience with Amazon, which if you think about it from first principles, makes sense given there is a dude delivering this stuff to your house. It's just that this convenience fee was hidden for the longest time as Amazon was growing its industry dominance. What's next? If they follow the Walmart model they will continue to squeeze suppliers and also push competitors out of business. So if you can, try to use alternatives.

comments.author: tedggh
comments.text: I use Amazon to buy cheap stuff like zip ties, printing paper and ink and some cleaning products. Almost every single major purchase I go directly to the manufacturer website or a specialized store. For example, I would never buy photography gear on Amazon. I go to Adorama or BH. For my favorite brands in say hiking or running gear I go to REI or RunningWarehouse or visit my local brick and mortar store. Amazon has truly become the convenience store for me, my average purchase is under $10. Almost everyone today offer free or inexpensive quick shipping and easy returns. They also have better customer service.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点：配達の予測可能性と返品の容易さがAmazonの価値だと指摘され、一方で価格プレミアムと低品質なサードパーティー商品への不満が挙げられた。賛否両論：賛成側は迅速で確実な配達と無条件返品が時間とリスクを削減すると評価し、批判側は同じ便利さを他店でも得られると主張し、Amazonの手数料が実質的「便利料金」だと指摘した。注目コメント：「配達予定日が95％の確率で守られる」という指摘は、物流の信頼性が価格以上の価値を生むという洞察を示し、多くの返信で共感された。

In our era of generative AI, that needs an update – "Believe nothing you see or hear, and only half of that over a strongly-authenticated channel from a reliable source". The story's themes of communities-of-mental-illness and blurred boundaries between doctor and patient (or betweentherapy and enablement) still resonate.

comments.text: I think I’m a little churlish about this whole “skeuomorphic museum exhibition” angle. I’ve worked in and with museum technology for 30 years, and run two businesses working with hundreds of cultural heritage / museum clients. Although this is technically impressive, I’m just not entirely sure why . Like - I just don’t want to dwell here… The whole idea that you have to be in some kind of virtual 3D space just seems a little bit 1998 for me. When I worked at the Science Museum in the early 2000’s for example we were thinking about VRML and I was out on gallery shooting 3D pans and knitting them together for the web. Back then it did feel like there was a “if you can’t visit, here’s the next best thing” and that this should be “a virtual reality space online”. But I think we’ve moved on. Museums have been making online exhibitions that are much more than just “a recreation of the real space online” for 20+ years - many of them are now really good at this. Take a look at someone like the Wellcome Collection [0] stories for example. They’re using the medium really well, they’re writing brilliantly, they’re knitting together fascinating relationships between items. The editorial is brilliant. The insights are brilliant. The linkages are brilliant. And as a consequence of all this, you end up wanting to stay. Not to knock the OP, it’s nice - I like it, it’s slick, it’s well done, and anyone who gets anything out the door deserves a pat on the back - but I’m not sure it works as an engaging mechanism. Not for me, anyway. [0] https://wellcomecollection.org/stories

On that note: getting the colors of the paintings right is also tricky. When you source these paintings you need to feed their color to a linearization process (as they likely will be in some non-linear color space like sRGB) before applying any scene lighting. comments.author: ollin
comments.text: Per The NVIDIA Way [1], the GeForce 256 was branded as "the first GPU" for marketing reasons alone; the actual first GPU was the subsequent GeForce 3 (which introduced programmable shaders): [Sanford] Russell grabbed Michael Hara for a thirty-minute brainstorm session to figure out how to market the GeForce 256 more effectively, and both executives remember coming out of the room with the notion to call the new chip the first entry in an entirely new product category altogether: a graphics processing unit, or GPU, which would be to graphics rendering what the computer's main central processing unit (CPU) was for all other computational tasks. Even so, the GPU moniker, when applied first to the GeForce 256, was controversial among Nvidia engineers, who pointed out that a chip could not truly be called a GPU unless it had several features that the GeForce 256 did not. The chip lacked a "state machine," a technical term meaning a dedicated processor that transitions from various states to execute and fetch instructions, in the same manner that a CPU does for programming commands. It was not programmable, meaning that graphics styles and features could not easily be customized by third-party developers. Instead, developers would have to rely on a fixed set of Nvidia-defined hardware functions. Moreover, the GeForce 256 did not have its own programming language. But the marketing team argued that such features were already planned for the next generation of graphics chips. And even without them, the GeForce 256 delivered a step change in performance that would be obvious to every gamer and computer enthusiast in the world. While not literally a GPU, the GeForce 256 could still be a category-defining product. The chips that would follow-the "true" GPUs that would be fully programmable by outside developers-were coming soon enough. So Nvidia's marketing team pushed forward with the GPU name over the dissent of Nvidia's engineers. "We don't need anyone's approval," Vivoli told them. He didn't think anyone outside of the industry would really care about the technical definition. Besides, "we knew the next one was going to be programmable. We decided to take a leap, make a stretch that this is a GPU." In February 2001, Nvidia released the GeForce 3, whose programmable shader technology and support for third-party development of its core graphics functions made it the first true GPU. [1] https://www.taekim.com

comments.author: joshkel
comments.text: I'm not clear on what the claim is here. The article faults LLMs for not being more creative (riding in the city in the rain, in East Asia, in outer space, etc.). But, if prompted, "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle," with no additional details or specification, then I would _expect_ something generic: a side view, nondescript terrain or perhaps terrain associated with a pelican (i.e., beach), little clothing (because birds don't wear clothes) with the possible exception of something strongly associated with bicyclists (a helmet). The article talks about "the LLM diversity collapse problem," which makes it sound like LLMs are getting less diverse over time, but the linked benchmarks suggest that newer, more capable models are _more_ creative. Out of curiosity, I tried a couple of prompt variations in Opus 5.5. "Be creative" did a beach scene but added fish to the bike basket and a lighthouse in the background - not too creative. "Pick a unique and creative variation of this concept" resulted in a "midnight circus act" of a pelican riding a penny-farthing on a tightrope while balancing a fishing pole with fish (and, this time, two lighthouses - the tightrope is implausibly strung between them).

comments.author: orbital-decay
comments.text: The lack of variety is probably the most underrated issue, and the most likely cause of annoying patterns you all hate. All current post-trained LLMs are mode-collapsed compared to the post-training set distribution, and this doesn't get nearly enough attention from the labs and independent researchers. It's far from being a transformer-only problem, it's a common failure mode in all kinds of models. It's not a fundamental limitation either, unsupervised models have no problem with being as diverse as the training set allows.

comments.text: It is fairly easy to go ask for a differently styled pelican, environment, background, etc. But that's not the point. (or, if undirected enough, as a collection of those based on a bog-standard architecture) Same-y enough that you could train an adversary on it? Or hack it afterward? I am beginning to think so!

comments.text: The example just doesn't support the claim. If I ask for a pelican riding a bicycle, I am expecting a relatively boring image of a pelican riding a bicycle, not a pelican flying through a thunderstorm while on a bicycle. That's just straight up not what I asked for. I didn't ask it to be creative, when I imagine myself riding a bicycle, I'm not flying! If I added "be creative and unique, you can add or change anything as long as there is still a pelican on a bicycle", then sure. Suppose I want an SVG of a laptop. It should probably look like a Macbook Air or something, neutral colors. Easily recognizable as a laptop. If it chose to be creative (unprompted) and gave me a futuristic or retro laptop, or one that's super wacky, there's a high chance of it looking bad, and a high chance I say "no that's not what i wanted". So during the training step, it probably learns to just follow instructions and be less creative unless asked. Sounds to me like LLMs are just getting better at following instructions and doing what they're told. Simple prompt, simple output.

stories.title_en: The Genealogy of Eliza
stories.title_ja: Elizaの系譜

comments.author: FrankWilhoit
comments.text: 1984, a friend of mine bought a Kaypro II and got a floppy with a BASIC ELIZA on it. We ran it and quickly found it shallow and anodyne. So we started looking at the files on the disk and found a dictionary file, which we opened. The first word in the dictionary was four letters long and began with an 'F'. "That's it," said my friend, "we just haven't been talking dirty enough to it."

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、1984年にKaypro IIで動作させたBASIC版ELIZAの単純さと、ディスク内の辞書ファイルを覗いたことで見つかった「F」で始まる4文字の単語（おそらく不適切語）への言及だ。投稿者はプログラムが浅薄で無害だと感じ、友人とともにソースを調査した結果、辞書の中身を発見し、それによって会話を「もっと汚い話題で」すれば反応が変わるだろうというジョークを交わした。賛否については、一部の読者はこうした初期チャットボットの内部構造を探る好奇心を肯定的に評価し、歴史的な技術的裏側に興味を示す一方、他方では不適切語を強調することがエルザの本質的な限界を軽視し、真の自然言語処理の難しさを見過ごす危険があると指摘している。特に注目されたコメントは、友人が「まだ十分に汚い話をしていないだけだ」と述べた発言で、これが当時のユーザーがエリザに期待した「深い理解」よりも表面的なパターンマッチングに依存していることを皮肉らしく示している点だ。
stories.editor_note: Elizaの系譜をたどると、初期チャットボットから現代のLLMまでの対話型AIの哲学的・技術的進化が見えてくる。日本の自然言語処理コミュニティでは、この歴史的文脈を教材として活用し、学生の理解を深めている。
